cards.title: equals() and hashCode(): The Contract, Why Both Are Mandatory, and How Violations Break Collections
cards.summary:
Every class in Java inherits two methods from Object: equals(Object) and hashCode(). equals() answers 'is this object logically the same as that one?' and hashCode() returns an int that hash-based collections (HashMap, HashSet, ConcurrentHashMap) use to pick which bucket the object should live in. By default, Object.equals() is simply reference equality (the == operator), and Object.hashCode() is derived from the object's identity (often from a memory-address-derived value; the exact algorithm is JVM-specific). Both defaults are consistent with each other, but they describe identity, not logical equality — which is almost never what you want for a domain object like User or Order.

The contract that every Java class must honor is stated in the Object class Javadoc: (1) equals must be reflexive (a.equals(a) is true), symmetric (if a.equals(b) then b.equals(a)), transitive (if a.equals(b) and b.equals(c) then a.equals(c)), and consistent (repeated calls return the same result unless the object changes); (2) if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(); (3) the reverse is not required — two unequal objects may share the same hashCode (that is a collision, and hash-based collections handle it by chaining or treeifying within the bucket). If a.equals(null) is called, it must return false, not throw.

The most common violation in interviews and real code is overriding equals() without overriding hashCode(). Because HashMap and HashSet use hashCode() first to find the bucket and equals() second to identify the exact key, two objects that are 'equal' but produce different hashCodes will land in different buckets and never be found — HashSet will happily store duplicates, and HashMap.get() will return null even though the key logically exists. Overriding hashCode() without equals() is less obviously broken (lookups still work via reference equality), but it collapses objects into fewer buckets and degrades performance toward O(n) chains. Symmetry is fragile if you mix getClass() with instanceof across subclasses — a superclass using instanceof and a subclass using instanceof can each report the other as equal from one direction only. The defensive rule is: use getClass() (not instanceof) in equals unless you deliberately follow Liskov substitution across subclasses, and always override both methods together.

A subtle real-world trap is using mutable fields in equals or hashCode. If a User object is added to a HashMap as a key, and later that User's email field (which participates in hashCode) is mutated, the object hashes into a different bucket on the next lookup — the entry is effectively lost. This is why map keys should be effectively immutable. Java records (Java 16+) auto-generate equals and hashCode based on all components, and using records for value objects eliminates a whole class of these bugs. If a developer asks 'why do we need to override both?', the strongest answer ties the contract to the two-stage lookup algorithm of hash collections: hashCode finds the neighborhood, equals finds the house.
bullets: equals() decides logical equality; hashCode() gives hash-based collections an int bucket index. Both are inherited from Object with identity-based defaults.
Contract: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(); the reverse is not required because collisions are handled within the bucket.
Overriding equals() without hashCode() breaks HashMap/HashSet — equal objects land in different buckets and become unreachable.
Use getClass() (not instanceof) in equals to preserve symmetry across subclasses, unless deliberately following Liskov substitution.
Never put mutable fields into equals/hashCode used as map keys — mutation after insertion makes the entry unreachable.
Java 16+ records auto-generate equals and hashCode from components; prefer records for value types.

cards.title: What Is a Thread? Lifecycle, States, and the start() vs run() Trap
cards.summary:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution that the operating system scheduler runs. On the JVM, every platform thread (the classic java.lang.Thread) maps one-to-one to an operating-system thread; that means creating a thread is not free — it costs a kernel call, a stack allocation (typically 512 KB to 1 MB by default), and OS bookkeeping. Virtual threads (Java 21+) break this mapping and are discussed in the Executor card. The critical mental model is process vs thread: a process owns its own isolated memory space (heap, code, statics); a thread shares the process's heap, code, and static fields with sibling threads, but each thread gets its own stack (for method frames and local variables) and its own program counter (the address of the next bytecode instruction to execute). This sharing is what makes threads powerful for coordination and also what makes them dangerous — any thread can corrupt a shared object unless you synchronize.

Java models thread state explicitly with the Thread.State enum: NEW (created but start() not yet called), RUNNABLE (executing or ready to execute — the OS decides when), BLOCKED (waiting to acquire a monitor lock held by another thread inside synchronized), WAITING (waiting indefinitely for another thread to act — Object.wait(), Thread.join() without timeout, LockSupport.park()), TIMED_WAITING (same as WAITING but with a deadline — Thread.sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), parkNanos), and TERMINATED (run() returned or threw). Understanding these states is how you diagnose deadlocks ('threads are in BLOCKED') versus slow responses ('threads are in WAITING on a lock or IO') versus CPU pressure ('threads are RUNNABLE').

The single most famous Java thread interview trap is start() versus run(). run() is just an ordinary method — calling it directly executes the method body on the calling thread, synchronously, with no new thread created. start() is the magic method that asks the JVM to allocate a new OS thread, set up the stack, and then invoke run() on that new thread. Calling t.run() instead of t.start() compiles, runs, and produces no error — the task simply executes on the caller's thread, defeating the point of threading. Every Java educator has seen production code with this bug.

There are three ways to give a thread work: extend Thread (not recommended because you burn your single inheritance slot on something that is not a domain concept), implement Runnable (the standard choice for fire-and-forget tasks), or implement Callable<V> (for tasks that return a value and may throw checked exceptions; you run these via ExecutorService.submit() and get a Future<V>). Two properties are worth knowing: daemon threads (created with t.setDaemon(true)) do not keep the JVM alive — when all user threads finish, the JVM exits and daemon threads are killed mid-task, which makes them suitable for background housekeeping but not for work you must not lose; thread priority (1–10) is a hint that the OS scheduler may completely ignore. Finally, context switches between threads are expensive (microseconds), so the goal is not 'more threads' but 'the right number of threads doing useful work' — which is exactly the problem the Executor framework solves.
bullets: A thread is the smallest schedulable unit of execution; classic threads map 1:1 to OS threads, sharing heap/statics but with their own stack and program counter.
Thread.State values: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor), WAITING (indefinite wait), TIMED_WAITING (with timeout), TERMINATED.
start() spawns a new OS thread and invokes run() on it; run() called directly runs on the current thread — classic interview trap.
Prefer Runnable (no return) or Callable<V> (returns value, can throw) over extending Thread.
Daemon threads do not prevent JVM shutdown; thread priority is only a scheduler hint and may be ignored.
Thread creation is not free (stack allocation + kernel call + context switch), which motivates thread pools.

cards.title: Executor Framework and ThreadPoolExecutor: Pooling, Rejection, and Sizing
cards.summary:
Creating a new Thread per request is expensive: each call allocates a stack (typically ~1 MB of virtual memory), makes a kernel call, and adds scheduler pressure. A service handling 5,000 requests per second cannot afford 5,000 new threads per second. The Executor framework (java.util.concurrent, Java 5+) solves this by decoupling task submission from thread management: you submit a Runnable or Callable to an ExecutorService, which queues it and hands it to one of a fixed set of reusable worker threads. The interface hides the pool; the concrete implementation ThreadPoolExecutor is where all the interesting knobs live, and understanding those knobs is what separates a junior answer from a senior one.

ThreadPoolExecutor has six constructor parameters that determine how it behaves: corePoolSize (threads kept alive even when idle), maximumPoolSize (hard ceiling), keepAliveTime (how long idle threads above corePoolSize live before being reclaimed), workQueue (a BlockingQueue where pending tasks wait), threadFactory (how threads are created — always name them for observability), and handler (a RejectedExecutionHandler deciding what to do when the pool is saturated). The internal task flow is a specific order that trips people up: (1) if fewer than corePoolSize threads are running, spawn a new thread immediately; (2) otherwise, try to enqueue the task in workQueue; (3) if the queue is full and running threads < maximumPoolSize, spawn another thread; (4) if the pool is at maximumPoolSize and the queue is full, invoke the rejection handler. Step 2 is critical — it means the queue is consulted before maximumPoolSize is reached, and if the queue is unbounded, maximumPoolSize is effectively never triggered.

The default Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) and Executors.newCachedThreadPool() are famously unsafe in production. newFixedThreadPool uses a LinkedBlockingQueue with Integer.MAX_VALUE capacity, so maximumPoolSize (set equal to n in that factory) is never the limiting factor — the queue grows without bound until you OutOfMemoryError. newCachedThreadPool uses a SynchronousQueue and sets maximumPoolSize to Integer.MAX_VALUE, so under sustained load it keeps spawning threads until the OS refuses. The correct pattern is to instantiate ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and an explicit RejectedExecutionHandler. AbortPolicy (the default) throws RejectedExecutionException to the caller; CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread execute the task itself (natural backpressure — the caller slows down); DiscardPolicy silently drops (dangerous); DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task (also usually wrong).

Sizing a pool is workload-dependent. For CPU-bound tasks (pure computation), a good starting point is the number of cores — more threads just create context-switch thrash. For IO-bound tasks (network calls, disk reads), threads spend most of their time parked, so you can oversubscribe: a common heuristic is cores × (1 + averageWaitTime / averageComputeTime). For a service where tasks wait 90% of the time on a downstream API, that ratio gives ~10 threads per core. Always validate with real load tests — the formula is a starting point, not a law. Shutdown matters too: shutdown() stops accepting new tasks and lets queued tasks finish, then terminates; shutdownNow() interrupts running tasks and returns the queued ones. Always call awaitTermination() with a timeout to avoid hanging your service shutdown. On Java 21+, virtual threads (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) change the game for IO-bound work: each task gets its own virtual thread, blocking calls unmount the virtual thread from its carrier OS thread, and you can run millions of concurrent tasks. For CPU-bound work, classic platform threads and sized pools remain the right tool.
bullets: ExecutorService decouples task submission from thread creation; ThreadPoolExecutor is the underlying implementation with all tuning parameters.
Task flow: core threads → workQueue → up to maximumPoolSize → rejection handler. The queue is consulted before maximum is reached.
Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so maximumPoolSize is effectively dead — OOM risk under sustained load.
Executors.newCachedThreadPool sets maximumPoolSize=Integer.MAX_VALUE — thread-explosion risk under sustained load.
Prefer explicit ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and CallerRunsPolicy (natural backpressure) for user-facing services.
Sizing: CPU-bound ≈ number of cores; IO-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute). Always load-test.
shutdown() drains gracefully; shutdownNow() interrupts; always awaitTermination() with a timeout.
Java 21+ virtual threads (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) make blocking IO cheap; keep sized platform-thread pools for CPU-bound work.

cards.title: CompletableFuture: Composing Async Work Without Blocking
cards.summary:
Future<V> (Java 5) represents a pending result: submit a Callable to an ExecutorService and you get back a Future, then call get() to block until the result is ready. That model breaks down for anything non-trivial, because Future has no composition — you cannot say 'when this finishes, transform the result, then combine it with another future, and if it fails, fall back.' You either block per future or build fragile manual coordination with CountDownLatch. CompletableFuture<V> (Java 8) adds both a completion-callback model and a full monadic composition toolkit, letting you express async pipelines declaratively the same way streams express data pipelines.

The creation primitives are supplyAsync(Supplier) (runs async, returns a value) and runAsync(Runnable) (runs async, returns CompletableFuture<Void>). Both take an optional Executor; if you omit it, they use ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which is a shared JVM-wide pool sized to the number of cores. That default is the source of many production incidents: a blocking IO task on the common pool starves every other part of the JVM using it. Always pass an explicit Executor for IO-bound stages.

Transformation and composition are where CompletableFuture earns its keep. thenApply(fn) transforms a successful result using a synchronous function and returns a new CompletableFuture<U>; thenApplyAsync(fn) runs the function on the executor pool instead of on whichever thread completed the previous stage. thenCompose(fn) is flatMap: fn returns another CompletableFuture, and thenCompose flattens the nesting (use this, not thenApply, when your function itself is async). thenCombine(other, fn) combines this future and another independent future once both complete. allOf(futures) returns a future that completes when all inputs complete; anyOf(futures) completes when the first one completes. Error handling uses exceptionally(fn) (recover from failure), handle(fn) (receive either result or exception, always runs), and whenComplete(fn) (side-effect observer that does not change the result). Java 9 added orTimeout and completeOnTimeout for deadline-aware pipelines.

The most damaging real-world trap is silent exception swallowing. If a stage throws and no exceptionally, handle, or whenComplete is attached anywhere downstream, the CompletableFuture completes exceptionally and the exception is never surfaced — no log, no crash, no visible symptom. The second-most common trap is a mental model error about which thread runs which stage: thenApply runs synchronously on whichever thread completed the previous stage (which could be the caller's thread, a pool thread, or even the main thread), whereas thenApplyAsync always dispatches to the pool. Mixing the two creates subtle thread-hopping bugs. Finally, get() throws checked InterruptedException and ExecutionException (requiring try/catch), while join() throws a single unchecked CompletionException — join is more ergonomic inside pipelines where you rarely expect checked exceptions.

CompletableFuture composes concurrent operations but does not provide backpressure. For streaming, high-fanout, or reactive workloads you should reach for Project Reactor (which backs Spring WebFlux) or RxJava, which model flows of events with explicit backpressure. For request-scoped fan-out (call 5 services in parallel, combine results) CompletableFuture is exactly the right tool and far simpler than a full reactive stack.
bullets: CompletableFuture adds composable callbacks and async pipelines to Future's blocking get().
supplyAsync returns a value; runAsync returns void. Always pass an explicit Executor for IO work — ForkJoinPool.commonPool() is shared and sized to CPU cores.
thenApply transforms synchronously on the completing thread; thenApplyAsync dispatches to the pool. thenCompose is flatMap for async functions.
Combine with thenCombine (two futures), allOf (wait for all), anyOf (wait for first).
Error handling: exceptionally (recover), handle (always runs), whenComplete (side-effect only). Exceptions are silently swallowed without one of these.
get() throws checked exceptions; join() throws a single unchecked CompletionException.
No backpressure — for streaming/reactive use Project Reactor (WebFlux) or RxJava.

cards.title: Comparable vs Comparator: Natural vs External Ordering, Contract, and Pitfalls
cards.summary:
Both interfaces express ordering, but they occupy different positions in the object's responsibility. Comparable<T> is implemented by the class itself (int compareTo(T other)) and defines the class's natural ordering — the single, canonical way to sort instances. Comparator<T> is external (int compare(T a, T b)) and lets callers define any number of alternative orderings without touching the class. Comparable answers 'how does an instance of this class line up against another by default?'; Comparator answers 'how does a caller want to sort these right now?'.

Use Comparable when the class has an obvious canonical order that will not change: String is lexicographic, Integer is numeric, LocalDate is chronological. Use Comparator when you need alternate orderings (sort users by age, then name, then salary), when the class is third-party and you cannot modify it, or when the ordering is context-dependent. You may define many Comparators per class; you may define only one Comparable natural ordering per class. Sorting a list of Comparables uses Collections.sort(list) or list.sort(null); sorting with a Comparator uses list.sort(comparator).

The contract for both methods is similar: compareTo (and compare) must return a negative int if this < other, zero if this == other, positive if this > other. Both must be consistent with equals in the following sense: a.compareTo(b) == 0 should imply a.equals(b) == true. This is not a compiler-enforced rule, but violating it causes silent data loss in TreeSet and TreeMap, which use compareTo/compare — not equals — to determine duplicate keys. If your User class sorts by email in compareTo but equality is by ID in equals, adding two users with the same email but different IDs to a TreeSet will silently drop the second one, because the tree treats them as the same element.

Modern Comparator factory methods (Java 8+) remove most of the boilerplate. Comparator.comparing(User::getName) builds a comparator from a key extractor; Comparator.comparingInt(User::getAge) avoids autoboxing; .thenComparing(...) chains a secondary sort; .reversed() flips the entire comparator; Comparator.nullsFirst(naturalOrder()) and Comparator.nullsLast(naturalOrder()) handle nulls safely. The classic bug that every interviewer checks for is the subtraction idiom: (a, b) -> a - b overflows for int when the difference exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (for example, Integer.MIN_VALUE - Integer.MAX_VALUE). Always use Integer.compare(a, b) or Comparator.comparingInt instead. A second trap: Collections.sort is a stable sort (TimSort since Java 7), so tasks with compare() returning 0 retain their original input order — this matters when chaining sort operations (sort by name first, then by age, and you get name-order preserved within each age group).
bullets: Comparable<T>.compareTo(T) defines natural ordering inside the class (one per class); Comparator<T>.compare(T, T) defines external ordering (many per class).
Use Comparable for canonical sorts (String, Integer, LocalDate); Comparator for alternate orderings and third-party classes.
TreeSet/TreeMap use compareTo/compare, not equals — inconsistent contracts silently merge unequal elements.
Java 8+ Comparator.comparing / thenComparing / reversed / nullsFirst replace verbose anonymous classes.
Never use (a, b) -> a - b — it overflows. Use Integer.compare or Comparator.comparingInt.
Collections.sort is stable (TimSort), so equal elements preserve input order across chained sorts.

cards.title: String Immutability, the String Pool, and StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
cards.summary:
String is a final class in java.lang whose instances are immutable: once created, the character sequence cannot be changed. Any operation that looks like modification — concat, replace, substring, trim, toUpperCase — returns a new String object and leaves the original untouched. (Under the hood, since Java 9 String stores bytes rather than chars, using Latin-1 encoding when all characters fit in 1 byte to save memory; the external behavior is unchanged.) Immutability is not an accident — it is a deliberate design choice that unlocks several guarantees at once.

First, thread safety for free: an immutable object can be shared across threads without any synchronization, because no thread can observe a half-modified state. Second, it enables the String pool (also called the intern pool), a JVM-managed cache of string literals. String literals like "hello" in source code are interned into this pool at class-load time, and identical literals across the codebase reference the same instance — a huge memory win for typical applications. Third, hashCode can be cached: String computes its hash once and stores it, making Strings exceptionally cheap as HashMap keys. Fourth, security: class names, connection URLs, file paths, and SQL strings cannot be tampered with after they are passed into a security-sensitive API.

The pool is where the == vs equals confusion originates. == compares references (are these the same object?), equals compares content (do these strings represent the same characters?). Because literals are interned, "hello" == "hello" is true — the compiler folds them to the same pooled instance. But new String("hello") explicitly allocates a fresh heap object outside the pool; that reference is != the interned literal, even though equals returns true. Calling s.intern() forces a string to be added to (or looked up in) the pool and returns the canonical instance. The interview rule is simple: never use == to compare String contents; use equals (or equalsIgnoreCase if case-insensitive is desired).

The two mutable companions differ in synchronization. StringBuilder is not synchronized — it is the default choice for building strings in a single thread, and it is typically 5–10x faster than StringBuffer under contention. StringBuffer is synchronized (all its methods are) and is only needed when the same buffer is genuinely shared across threads. Concatenation with += in a loop is the classic performance bug: each iteration allocates a new String and copies all previous characters, giving O(n²) total work. The fix is to accumulate into a StringBuilder and call toString() once. (Note that in modern Java, single-statement concatenation like "a" + x + "b" is compiled efficiently via invokedynamic / StringConcatFactory, but the loop case still degrades quadratically.) A final, security-oriented trap: never store passwords in a String. Because strings are immutable and cached, the password stays in heap memory (and in heap dumps, and in swap) until the GC collects it, which could be a long time. Use char[] instead — you can zero out the array immediately after use with Arrays.fill(password, '\0').
bullets: String is immutable — every 'modification' returns a new instance; safe to share across threads.
Immutability enables the String pool (interned literals), cached hashCode, and security guarantees.
== compares references, equals compares content. Literals are pooled; new String("...") creates a fresh heap object.
intern() forces a string into the pool and returns the canonical instance.
StringBuilder: mutable, not thread-safe, fast. StringBuffer: mutable, synchronized, slower. Use StringBuilder by default.
s += "x" in a loop is O(n²) — each iteration allocates and copies. Use StringBuilder.
Passwords in String persist in heap until GC and appear in dumps; use char[] and zero it after use.

cards.title: What Is Spring and Why Do IoC and DI Exist?
cards.summary:
Spring is a Java framework whose central purpose is to remove the burden of manually creating and wiring objects inside your code. Before Spring, a typical service looked like this: OrderService creates its own PaymentClient with new, PaymentClient creates its own HttpClient, and the UserRepository builds its own database connection pool. Every class controls its own dependencies, which means every class must know how its dependencies are constructed, and swapping a real dependency for a fake one in a test requires editing production code. This is not just ugly — it makes testing painful, makes configuration scattered across hundreds of files, and makes it impossible for a framework to manage the lifecycle of anything.

Inversion of Control (IoC) is the principle that flips this responsibility. Instead of each object asking for its dependencies, a central container is responsible for creating objects, injecting their dependencies, and managing their lifecycle. The object simply declares what it needs; the container figures out how to provide it. Dependency Injection (DI) is the specific technique Spring uses to implement IoC: dependencies are passed into an object from outside (usually through a constructor, a setter, or a field) rather than created inside the object. IoC is the goal, DI is the mechanism, and the Spring IoC container is the machinery that does it.

A useful analogy: imagine running a restaurant. Without IoC, every chef must personally shop for ingredients, sharpen their own knives, and repair the stove before cooking. With IoC, a central kitchen manager (the container) ensures that when the chef walks in, ingredients are stocked, knives are sharp, and the stove is ready. The chef only declares 'I need vegetables and a clean cutting board' and the manager provides them. If the manager wants to substitute a different supplier, the chef never knows. This is exactly what Spring does for Java objects.

The practical benefits are concrete: (1) Testability — you can pass a mock PaymentClient into OrderService in a unit test without changing OrderService's code. (2) Loose coupling — OrderService depends on the PaymentClient interface, and the implementation can be swapped by configuration alone. (3) Lifecycle management — the container knows when beans are created, initialized, and destroyed, so it can run @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy hooks. (4) Configuration centralization — instead of new calls scattered everywhere, dependencies are declared once in configuration and managed uniformly. (5) Cross-cutting concerns — because the container creates the objects, it can wrap them with proxies for transactions, security, caching, or logging (this is how @Transactional works).

The interview-critical mental model is: Spring is not a library you call; it is a container that owns your objects. When you write @Service on OrderService, you are saying 'this class is a bean — please instantiate it, resolve its constructor arguments from other beans you manage, and hand me the finished instance whenever I ask for OrderService'. Everything else in Spring — auto-configuration, AOP, @Transactional, Spring Boot — is built on top of this container. If you understand the container, the rest of Spring becomes a set of conveniences rather than magic.
bullets: IoC (Inversion of Control) means the container, not your code, controls object creation and lifecycle.
DI (Dependency Injection) is the technique: dependencies are passed in, not created inside the object.
Spring IoC container = BeanFactory / ApplicationContext that creates beans, resolves dependencies, and manages lifecycle.
Benefits: testability (inject mocks), loose coupling (depend on interfaces), lifecycle hooks, centralized config, proxy-based cross-cutting concerns.
The container owns your beans — you declare what you need, it provides it.
Everything in Spring Boot (@Transactional, @Cacheable, security, auto-config) is built on the container.

cards.title: How Dependency Injection Actually Works Inside Spring
cards.summary:
Dependency Injection feels magical the first time: you write @Service on a class, @Autowired on a constructor, and somehow the object appears with all its dependencies ready. The truth is that Spring performs a very specific set of steps, all driven by reflection and metadata that it collects during startup. Understanding this flow is what separates 'I use Spring' from 'I know Spring'.

The story begins with the BeanDefinition. During startup, Spring scans your classpath for annotated classes (@Component and its specializations @Service, @Repository, @Controller), parses any @Configuration classes, and reads XML if present. For each candidate, it creates a BeanDefinition object — a recipe describing the class name, scope, constructor arguments, property values, lazy-init flag, and lifecycle callbacks. Importantly, no beans are instantiated during this phase; only recipes are collected. These recipes are stored in a BeanFactory (usually DefaultListableBeanFactory), which is a registry keyed by bean name.

Once the recipes are collected, the container performs the actual instantiation. It first sorts beans topologically by dependency: if OrderService needs PaymentClient, PaymentClient must be created first. For each bean, Spring: (1) resolves the constructor to use — either the single constructor, or the one marked @Autowired, or the one selected by @ConstructorProperties or autowire constructor matching; (2) resolves each constructor parameter — by type in the bean registry; if multiple candidates exist, it uses @Qualifier, @Primary, or bean name matching to disambiguate; (3) instantiates the bean via reflection (Class.getDeclaredConstructor(...).newInstance(args)); (4) populates @Autowired fields and setters; (5) runs BeanPostProcessors before initialization (@PostConstruct, InitializingBean, custom init-method); (6) runs BeanPostProcessors after initialization — this is where AOP proxies are wrapped around the bean; (7) caches the finished bean in the singleton registry by name.

Three injection styles exist. Constructor injection (recommended): dependencies are passed via constructor arguments and can be marked final, making the bean immutable and guaranteeing it is never half-constructed. Field injection (@Autowired on a field): Spring uses reflection to set the field after construction — it is easy to write but hides dependencies, prevents final fields, and makes the class impossible to construct in a plain unit test without reflection. Setter injection: allows optional dependencies and reconfiguration, but lets the bean exist in an incompletely initialized state. The modern recommendation (and what Spring itself does internally since 4.3) is constructor injection; Spring even auto-detects the single-arg constructor without requiring @Autowired.

Failure modes matter for the interview. BeanCreationException: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException when a required dependency has no matching bean — the message contains the exact parameter name and type. NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException when two beans of the same type exist and no @Qualifier/@Primary resolves them. Circular dependency errors when constructor injection forms a cycle (A needs B needs A). BeanCurrentlyInCreationException when the same bean is requested recursively — Spring detects the loop and fails fast rather than looping forever. Understanding these errors is more important than understanding the happy path, because every production issue manifests as one of them.
bullets: Startup = collect BeanDefinitions (recipes), then instantiate topologically, resolving constructor parameters by type.
Instantiation uses reflection: Class.getDeclaredConstructor(...).newInstance(args).
Three injection styles: constructor (recommended — immutable, testable), field (hides deps), setter (optional deps).
Disambiguation: @Qualifier → @Primary → bean name match. If none resolves, NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.
Missing bean → NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. Cycle in constructor injection → BeanCurrentlyInCreationException.
BeanPostProcessors run after initialization — this is where AOP proxies are wrapped around the finished bean.
cards.code:
Startup pipeline (simplified)

1. ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner -> finds @Component classes
2. @Configuration classes parsed -> @Bean methods become recipes
3. BeanFactory stores BeanDefinition{ name, class, scope, deps, ... }
4. Topological sort by dependency
5. For each bean:
   a. Resolve constructor (single / @Autowired / param matching)
   b. Resolve each parameter by type in bean registry
      - multiple candidates? @Qualifier / @Primary / name match
   c. Reflectively instantiate
   d. Populate @Autowired fields / setters
   e. BeanPostProcessor.beforeInit  -> @PostConstruct
   f. BeanPostProcessor.afterInit   -> AOP proxies wrapped here
   g. Store in singletonObjects cache

Common exceptions

NoSuchBeanDefinitionException : no bean of the required type
NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException : multiple candidates, no qualifier
BeanCurrentlyInCreationException : circular constructor dependency

cards.title: Bean Lifecycle and Scopes: From Instantiation to Destruction
cards.summary:
Every bean Spring manages passes through a well-defined lifecycle. The full sequence is: instantiation (constructor runs) → populate properties (@Autowired fields and setters are set) → BeanNameAware.setBeanName → BeanFactoryAware.setBeanFactory → ApplicationContextAware.setApplicationContext → BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization → @PostConstruct method → InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet → custom init-method (from @Bean(initMethod=...) or XML) → BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization → bean is now ready and cached for use → at shutdown: @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy → custom destroy-method → bean is removed.

The most interview-important stage is BeanPostProcessor — because this is where Spring wraps the bean in AOP proxies. @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, and @PreAuthorize all work by installing a BeanPostProcessor that inspects the finished bean and, if it sees the annotation, returns a proxy wrapping the original. This is why a call to a @Transactional method from outside the class is intercepted, but a self-invocation inside the same class is not — the self-call bypasses the proxy. Knowing this chain explains most 'why doesn't @Transactional work here' questions.

Scopes determine the lifetime and sharing model of a bean. singleton (default): exactly one instance per Spring container; the same object is returned every time it is requested. This is the source of the classic bug where a developer stores request-specific data in a singleton field and it 'leaks' between requests — singletons must be stateless or thread-safe. prototype: a new instance every time the bean is requested; Spring does NOT manage destruction of prototype beans, so @PreDestroy does not run for them. request: one instance per HTTP request (web-aware contexts only). session: one instance per HTTP session. application: one instance per ServletContext (similar to singleton but scoped to the web application). websocket: one instance per WebSocket session.

The singleton-scoped-bean-depends-on-request-scoped-bean problem is a frequent interview question. If a singleton bean has an @Autowired field of a request-scoped bean, the singleton captures whatever instance was available at injection time — which is either wrong or a proxy. Spring solves this with scoped proxies: annotating the request-scoped bean with @Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) makes the container inject a proxy that resolves the real request-scoped bean on every call. The proxy delegates to the correct instance for the current request thread. Without this, the singleton holds a stale reference.

Finally, initialization and destruction ordering matters when beans depend on each other. If BeanA depends on BeanB, Spring destroys BeanA before BeanB (reverse of creation). @PreDestroy is a JSR-250 annotation processed by CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor; on shutdown the order is @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy → custom destroy-method. In Spring Boot with graceful shutdown enabled (server.shutdown=graceful), the embedded server stops accepting new requests, waits for in-flight requests, then triggers context shutdown so @PreDestroy hooks can flush caches, close connections, and complete in-flight work cleanly.
bullets: Lifecycle: construct → populate → Aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessor.before → @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet → init-method → BeanPostProcessor.after → use → @PreDestroy → destroy → destroy-method.
AOP proxies (@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize) are installed during BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization.
Scopes: singleton (one per container), prototype (new each get, no destroy callback), request, session, application, websocket.
Singletons must be stateless or thread-safe — shared mutable state leaks between requests.
Injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton requires a scoped proxy (@Scope(proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS)).
Destruction is the reverse of creation order; @PreDestroy runs before DisposableBean.destroy before custom destroy-method.
Spring Boot graceful shutdown: stop accepting → drain in-flight → close context → run destroy hooks.

cards.title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository: Semantics, Real Differences, and the Persistence Exception Trick
bullets: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller are all stereotypes — meta-annotated with @Component, so bean registration is identical.
@Service is purely semantic — no runtime behavior; it labels business logic.
@Repository adds exception translation (native SQL/JPA exceptions → Spring DataAccessException) via PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor.
@Controller enables MVC handler mapping; @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody.
Spring Data JPA auto-applies @Repository to interface-based repositories, so hand-written @Repository is rare.
Use @Component as the generic catch-all when the class does not fit a specific stereotype; utility classes with only static methods should not be beans at all.

cards.title: @Autowired Resolution: Type First, Then Qualifier, Primary, Name
bullets: @Autowired resolves by type first, not by name — this is the most common misunderstanding.
Resolution chain: unique type → @Qualifier → @Primary → bean-name fallback (needs -parameters) → error.
Constructor injection (recommended) makes deps final, fails fast, and enables plain-Java tests. Single-constructor case does not need @Autowired.
Field injection hides dependencies, prevents final, and NPEs in unit tests without a Spring context.
Optional<T> / @Autowired(required=false) / ObjectProvider<T> handle optional or lazily-resolved dependencies.
@Lazy defers resolution — useful for cycles and expensive beans.
NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException = multiple candidates, no qualifier/primary. NoSuchBeanDefinitionException = no candidate.

cards.title: Circular Dependencies: Why They Break, How Spring Works Around Them, and Why You Should Still Avoid Them
cards.summary:
A circular dependency exists when bean A depends on bean B and bean B depends back on bean A. With constructor injection, this is impossible to satisfy: to construct A, you need B; to construct B, you need A; neither can be created first. Spring detects this and throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException at startup with a message naming the cycle. The correct answer in an interview is not 'Spring handles it' — it is 'Spring only handles it for setter and field injection, and even then it is a design smell you should refactor away'.

For constructor injection, there is no workaround — Spring refuses to construct the cycle and fails fast. This is actually a feature: constructor cycles almost always indicate a real design problem (two services too tightly coupled). The fix is to extract a third component, introduce an event-based interaction, or move one of the responsibilities so the dependency direction is one-way. Refactoring is the right answer; do not reach for @Lazy to make a constructor cycle compile.

For setter and field injection, Spring uses a workaround centered on the three-level cache of singletons. When Spring needs to construct A and A depends on B (via field or setter), the algorithm is: (1) instantiate A using its no-arg constructor — A now exists but is incompletely initialized; (2) record A in the 'singletonFactories' cache as an ObjectFactory that can produce A (or its early proxy); (3) resolve A's field B — B needs A, so Spring looks up A; (4) since A is already in singletonFactories, Spring calls the factory to get the early A reference, and puts it in 'earlySingletonObjects'; (5) B gets the early A, completes, moves to singletonObjects; (6) A continues, receives B, completes, moves to singletonObjects. The three caches (singletonObjects, earlySingletonObjects, singletonFactories) are how Spring ensures a single shared instance even during the cycle.

AOP proxies complicate this. If A is @Transactional or @Async, the bean that other beans see is the proxy, not the raw A. During a cycle, the early reference Spring hands out must be the proxy, not the raw instance — otherwise B would end up holding a reference to the un-proxied A and calls like @Transactional would silently bypass the interceptor. Spring handles this by making singletonFactories return the early proxy if an AOP proxy is planned for A. This is exactly why the design has three levels rather than two: singletonFactories can decide, at the moment of exposure, whether to expose the raw bean or a proxy. If you have ever seen 'BeanCurrentlyInCreationException' with a mention of 'Bean with name X has been injected into other beans [...] in its raw version', this is the scenario Spring is warning about — a cycle where the early reference cannot be a proxy, potentially causing AOP to silently not apply.

In Spring Boot 2.6+, circular references are disabled by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false), and enabling them is a deliberate configuration. The reason is exactly the design smell: cycles indicate tangled dependency graphs that are hard to test, hard to reason about, and full of subtle bugs (unfinished initialization, AOP bypass, initialization-order nondeterminism). The correct long-term answer is to refactor: extract a common interface into a third bean, use ApplicationEventPublisher for loose coupling, or restructure the domain. In interviews, the strongest answer is 'Spring can break the cycle for field/setter injection using its three-level singleton cache, but the right response is to refactor — cycles hide design problems and break in surprising ways with AOP and proxying'.
bullets: Constructor injection cycles fail immediately with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException — no workaround. Refactor is the answer.
Field/setter cycles are resolved via a three-level singleton cache: singletonObjects, earlySingletonObjects, singletonFactories.
The early exposure of a partially initialized bean is what breaks the cycle — other beans receive a reference before A finishes construction.
AOP proxies must be applied to the early reference too, or @Transactional/@Async silently bypass — this is why singletonFactories exists as a separate layer.
Spring Boot 2.6+ disables circular references by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false) because cycles indicate design problems.
Refactoring options: extract a third bean, use ApplicationEventPublisher, or restructure to enforce one-way dependency direction.

cards.title: AOP: JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB, Where @Transactional Lives, and Why It Silently Fails
cards.summary:
Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) is the idea that some concerns cut across many classes — transactions, logging, security, caching, metrics — and should not be copy-pasted into every method. AOP lets you declare 'for every method annotated with @Transactional, wrap it in begin-commit-rollback logic' in one place, and applies it uniformly at runtime. Spring implements AOP not with bytecode weaving at build time (like AspectJ), but with runtime proxies: the container instantiates your class, then hands the finished instance to a BeanPostProcessor that returns a proxy object wrapping the original. External callers talk to the proxy; the proxy decides whether and how to invoke the original.

There are two proxy mechanisms and the choice between them determines the failure modes you will hit. JDK dynamic proxy works only against interfaces: given an interface Foo, java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class[]{Foo.class}, handler) returns a new class that implements Foo and forwards every call to an InvocationHandler. Spring's default behavior is: if the bean implements at least one interface, wrap it in a JDK proxy. The consequence is that callers who inject the concrete class (not the interface) will fail with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException at startup, because the bean in the container is a proxy that only implements the interface, not a subclass of the concrete class.

CGLIB (Code Generation Library) generates a subclass of the target class at runtime using bytecode manipulation, overriding every non-final method to route through the interceptor. This works without interfaces, which is why Spring Boot 2.x defaults to proxyTargetClass=true — @Transactional on a class without interfaces just works. The limitation is that CGLIB cannot proxy final classes, final methods, or private methods, because it cannot subclass final classes or override final methods. If you put @Transactional on a final method, the annotation is silently ignored and the method runs without a transaction. This is one of the most common production bugs with Spring AOP.

The other huge trap is self-invocation. If OrderService.process() (proxied, @Transactional) calls this.validate() (also @Transactional), the call goes this → validate on the same object, bypassing the proxy entirely. No new transaction, no interceptor. Every Java developer eventually debugs this, so an interview answer that mentions self-invocation is strongly preferred. The fixes: extract validate() into a separate bean, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ load-time weaving (which does not use proxies).

Multiple aspects applying to the same method are ordered by @Order or by Ordered interface. Lower values run first on the way in and last on the way out. @Transactional defaults to Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE so that security and caching aspects run outside the transaction boundary — if the security check fails, no transaction is started, which is the desired behavior. Getting the order wrong (e.g., putting caching inside the transaction) means a cache hit still opens a transaction, wasting a connection.

The mental model to take into an interview: Spring AOP = proxy wrapping + invocation handler + reflection. Everything else (@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, @Retryable, custom @Aspect) is a different interceptor sitting on the same proxy. If the proxy is not called (self-invocation), or cannot be created (final class/method), or is bypassed (calling the raw target by reflection), the aspect does not apply — silently.
bullets: Spring AOP uses runtime proxies, not compile-time weaving; a BeanPostProcessor wraps the finished bean in a proxy that callers receive instead of the raw object.
JDK dynamic proxy: interface-only, uses java.lang.reflect.Proxy + InvocationHandler; default when the bean implements an interface.
CGLIB: generates a subclass, overrides non-final methods; default in Spring Boot 2+ (proxyTargetClass=true); cannot proxy final classes, final methods, or private methods.
Self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy — @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, and @PreAuthorize silently do not apply.
Aspect ordering uses @Order / Ordered; @Transactional defaults to LOWEST_PRECEDENCE so auth and caching sit outside the transaction.
Every Spring AOP annotation is just a different interceptor on the same proxy — understand the proxy, understand them all.

cards.title: @Configuration and proxyBeanMethods: Why Calling a @Bean Method Does Not Create a Second Instance
cards.summary:
A @Configuration class with @Bean methods is where you declare beans programmatically. The naive expectation is that each call to a @Bean method creates a new object — but with the default proxyBeanMethods=true, calling dataSource() from another @Bean method inside the same @Configuration returns the same singleton instance that Spring has already cached, not a new one. This is not magic; it works because Spring subclasses the @Configuration class at startup via CGLIB and overrides every @Bean method so that the first call is intercepted and cached in the singleton registry; subsequent calls return the cached instance without executing the method body again.

Concretely, if you write: @Configuration class AppConfig { @Bean DataSource ds() {...} @Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc() { return new JdbcTemplate(ds()); } } — the jdbc() method calls ds() directly. Without the CGLIB subclass, that call would run ds()'s body again, producing a second DataSource outside Spring's control. With the CGLIB subclass, the overridden ds() checks the container first: if the bean already exists, return it; if not, invoke super.ds(), register the result, and return. The result is that both the bean registry and any direct method calls share one instance. This is what 'proxyBeanMethods' names.

Setting @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) disables the CGLIB subclass. Spring calls this 'lite mode'. Lite mode is faster to start (no bytecode generation per @Configuration class) and is fine when your @Bean methods do not call each other. But if they do call each other, each call produces a new instance — resulting in silent duplicate beans, duplicate connections, duplicate thread pools. Spring Boot 3's own auto-configurations use proxyBeanMethods=false because they are carefully written to inject MethodParameter-based dependencies (ObjectProvider<DataSource>) instead of calling sibling @Bean methods, but user code that copies the pattern without the discipline gets burned. Rule of thumb: keep proxyBeanMethods=true (the default) unless you have measured startup cost and verified no cross-bean-method calls.

A related distinction: @Component + @Bean is not a @Configuration class. If you put @Bean methods inside a plain @Component class, the class is never subclassed, and direct calls between @Bean methods always produce new instances — even without proxyBeanMethods=false. This is called 'lite mode by accident' and is a very common bug. The rule is simple: @Bean methods belong in @Configuration classes; anything else is a trap.

One more gotcha: @Bean methods inside @Configuration cannot be static in normal cases — static @Bean methods are allowed but they run before the configuration class itself is instantiated, which means they cannot see the surrounding config class's state or other @Bean instances (except through BeanFactoryAware injection). Static @Bean methods bypass the CGLIB override entirely, so calling them from sibling methods always creates new instances.

To verify what Spring actually did, enable debug logging on org.springframework.context and look for 'Enhanced configuration class' lines — they appear for each @Configuration class that was subclassed. If you set proxyBeanMethods=false or used a plain @Component, those lines will not appear, and any cross-method @Bean calls are duplicating work.
bullets: @Configuration default (proxyBeanMethods=true) triggers CGLIB subclassing; @Bean methods are overridden to return the cached singleton on subsequent calls.
Direct calls like jdbc(ds()) from one @Bean to another return the same instance — no duplicate beans.
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) = lite mode: faster startup, but direct cross-method @Bean calls create duplicate instances.
Putting @Bean methods inside a plain @Component also disables the proxy — a silent source of duplicate beans.
Static @Bean methods bypass CGLIB entirely — calling them from sibling @Bean methods always creates new instances.
Spring Boot 3 auto-configs use proxyBeanMethods=false because they never call sibling @Bean methods — copy that pattern only if you have the same discipline.

cards.title: BeanPostProcessor vs BeanFactoryPostProcessor: The Extension Points That Build Spring Itself
cards.summary:
Spring is a small core surrounded by extension points. Almost every feature you think of as 'built into Spring' — @Autowired, @PostConstruct, @Transactional, @Configuration, exception translation, MVC, caching, async — is installed by an implementor of one of two interfaces: BeanFactoryPostProcessor (BFPP) and BeanPostProcessor (BPP). Knowing these two is the difference between treating Spring as a black box and understanding exactly where each feature attaches.

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor runs very early, before any non-BFPP bean is instantiated. It receives the ConfigurableListableBeanFactory and can inspect and modify BeanDefinitions — the recipes, not the beans. This is when Spring resolves placeholders (${...}), processes @PropertySource, and lets @Configuration classes be parsed. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor is the canonical BFPP: it reads every BeanDefinition, finds @Configuration classes and @Bean methods, and registers their recipes before the container starts instantiating beans. PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer is another: it replaces ${...} placeholders in bean property values with values from property sources.

A BeanPostProcessor runs per bean, during the instantiation of every other bean. It has two hooks: postProcessBeforeInitialization(bean, name) — runs before @PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, and custom init-method — and postProcessAfterInitialization(bean, name) — runs after all init hooks and is expected to return the bean that will be stored in the container. Crucially, whatever the after-init hook returns becomes the bean; return a proxy and callers get the proxy. This is exactly how @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, and validation work: AbstractAutoProxyCreator (a BPP) inspects the finished bean, finds matching advice, and returns a proxy wrapping the original. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor is a BPP: it walks the bean's fields and setters and injects dependencies during the before-init phase. CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor is a BPP: it discovers and invokes @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy.

The ordering rule matters in practice: BPPs themselves are instantiated early, before the rest of the beans, so they must be declared as @Bean static methods (or registered via BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor) if they need to modify beans during the main instantiation. A common warning at startup — 'Bean X is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying)' — happens when a BPP (or a bean a BPP depends on) is instantiated too early to be wrapped by other BPPs. That warning usually means @Transactional or @Async will not apply to the affected bean.

When the two phases interact badly, the result is subtle. If your BFPP declares beans conditionally based on properties, they will not be visible to BPPs that were instantiated before the BFPP ran. If your BPP tries to inject a bean via @Autowired, it will likely trigger early instantiation of that bean, cascading the 'not eligible for auto-proxying' warning across the graph. The safe rule: BFPPs should not depend on regular beans; BPPs should not depend on regular beans either, or must use ObjectProvider<T> for lazy resolution.

In an interview, the strongest answer describes the two phases in order (BFPP: modify recipes before any bean; BPP: wrap each bean during instantiation), names a concrete BPP for each Spring feature (AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor for @Autowired, CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor for @PostConstruct, AbstractAutoProxyCreator for AOP), and explains the early-instantiation gotcha. That demonstrates you know Spring's extension architecture, not just its annotations.
bullets: BFPP (BeanFactoryPostProcessor): runs before any bean is instantiated; can read/modify BeanDefinitions (recipes). ConfigurationClassPostProcessor and PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer are canonical examples.
BPP (BeanPostProcessor): runs per bean; before-init (@PostConstruct discovery) and after-init (AOP proxy wrapping). Whatever after-init returns becomes the bean.

AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor installs @Autowired/@Value injection; CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor invokes @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy; AbstractAutoProxyCreator installs @Transactional/@Cacheable/@Async proxies.
BPPs are instantiated early — declare them as @Bean static or via BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor when they need to modify other beans during startup.
The 'not eligible for auto-proxying' warning means a bean was created before a BPP could wrap it — @Transactional/@Async will silently not apply.
Safe rule: BFPPs and BPPs should not inject regular beans (use ObjectProvider<T>) — otherwise they trigger early instantiation and the warning cascade.

cards.title: What Is Spring Boot and Why Does It Exist on Top of Spring?
cards.summary:
Spring Framework, for all its power, is painful to start a project with. Setting up a web app in vanilla Spring requires: an XML file or a @Configuration class for the DispatcherServlet, a servlet container (Tomcat) downloaded and configured separately, a Jackson ObjectMapper configured correctly, a DataSource bean wired to a database driver, a transaction manager, a connection pool, plus manually curated dependency versions in Maven or Gradle. The problem is not that any one step is hard — it is that every new Spring project requires all of them, and every version mismatch between Spring 5.3.x, Jackson 2.13.x, Hibernate 5.6.x, and Tomcat 9 is a debugging session waiting to happen.

Spring Boot's core thesis is Convention over Configuration: pick sensible defaults for common choices, let the developer override only what they care about, and make the whole thing runnable as a single jar. Concretely, Spring Boot contributes four things on top of Spring: (1) Starters — curated dependency bundles (spring-boot-starter-web pulls Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat, and validation, all version-compatible); (2) Auto-configuration — Spring Boot inspects what is on the classpath and configures beans automatically (if H2 is on the classpath and no DataSource bean exists, Boot creates an in-memory one); (3) An embedded server — Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow is packaged inside the jar, so `java -jar app.jar` is a runnable web server with no external install; (4) Actuator — production features like health checks, metrics, and environment inspection out of the box.

The distinction people get wrong: Spring Boot is NOT a replacement for Spring. It is Spring — the same ApplicationContext, the same @Service, @Autowired, @Transactional, the same AOP, the same bean lifecycle. Spring Boot adds a launcher (@SpringBootApplication), a dependency management layer, a classpath-driven auto-configuration mechanism, and production defaults. If you are debugging a @Transactional issue in a Spring Boot app, you are using Spring's @Transactional — Boot does not change how it works. If you are debugging circular dependencies, you are using Spring's bean lifecycle — Boot only sets allow-circular-references=false by default.

A good analogy: vanilla Spring is a fully stocked professional kitchen where you must organize every utensil yourself; Spring Boot is the same kitchen pre-arranged with a default layout, common ingredients stocked, and a recipe book open on the counter — you can rearrange anything, but the default setup gets you cooking in five minutes. The kitchen is the same; the arrangement is different.

The interview-relevant mental model: @SpringBootApplication on a main class is a composed annotation of @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration class), @EnableAutoConfiguration (turn on classpath-driven bean provisioning), and @ComponentScan (scan the current package and below). When main() calls SpringApplication.run(...), Boot builds an ApplicationContext, runs auto-configuration, starts the embedded server, and fires ApplicationReadyEvent. Everything else — starters, actuators, embedded Tomcat — is a layer on that context. If you understand the context, you understand the app; if you understand only the annotations, you are memorizing.
bullets: Spring Boot is Spring + convention over configuration; same IoC container, same annotations, same AOP.
Four contributions on top of Spring: starters (curated deps), auto-configuration (classpath-driven beans), embedded server, Actuator.
@SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.
The embedded server means java -jar app.jar is a fully self-contained web application — no external Tomcat.
If you are debugging a bean or a transaction in Spring Boot, you are debugging Spring — Boot does not change that behavior.

cards.title: What Happens Inside Spring Boot During Startup: Step-by-Step Sequence
cards.summary:
When you call SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args), Spring Boot executes a well-defined sequence that lasts from 'JVM started main' to 'ApplicationReadyEvent fired and the port is listening'. Understanding this sequence is what lets you debug slow startups, order-of-initialization bugs, and 'why did my bean get created before that other bean?' problems.

The sequence, in order: (1) SpringApplication constructs — it inspects the classpath to guess the application type (SERVLET, REACTIVE, or NONE), discovers listeners via spring.factories / META-INF/spring.factories, and detects the main class. (2) The application starts an Environment — property sources (system properties, environment variables, application.yml, application-{profile}.yml, command-line args) are loaded in priority order. (3) The banner is printed. (4) ApplicationContext is created — AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext for a typical Spring MVC app. (5) ApplicationContextInitializers run — user-supplied hooks that can modify the context before beans are loaded. (6) Environment-prepared listeners fire. (7) The context is refreshed: this is the big one. It triggers ConfigurationClassPostProcessor (parses @Configuration classes, discovers @ComponentScan targets, evaluates @Conditional, registers @Bean definitions from auto-configuration), then instantiates all singletons in dependency order, runs BeanPostProcessors (which install @Autowired, @PostConstruct, AOP proxies), and finally starts the embedded web server. (8) ContextRefreshedEvent fires. (9) ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner beans run — with @Order determining sequence. (10) ApplicationReadyEvent fires; the app is now serving traffic.

The most common startup failure modes map to these phases. Missing bean errors (NoSuchBeanDefinitionException) happen during step 7 when bean instantiation runs. Port-in-use errors (WebServerException: Unable to start embedded Tomcat) happen during the server-start sub-phase of step 7 — after all beans have been created. Configuration exceptions (invalid properties, failed @ConfigurationProperties binding) surface during step 7's bean instantiation, especially for beans that fail-fast. ApplicationRunner exceptions run AFTER the web server is up — if one throws, the app has already started listening and will only begin shutting down because of the error.

The banner is a nice diagnostic marker: if you see the banner but no 'Tomcat started on port 8080', you know you failed during context refresh. If you see 'Tomcat started' but nothing serving, the issue is probably downstream (ApplicationRunner throwing, then triggering shutdown) or a filter chain misconfiguration.

Two startup-tuning facts matter in production. First, lazy initialization (spring.main.lazy-initialization=true, or @Lazy per bean) defers non-critical bean creation until first use — startups go from 30s to 3s in large apps, at the cost of first-request latency spikes and delayed failure detection. Second, startup failures are much easier to diagnose with debug logging (logging.level.root=DEBUG or --debug on the command line): Boot prints an auto-configuration report ('Positive matches', 'Negative matches', 'Exclusions') that lists exactly which conditions failed and why.

An interview answer that names the phases in order, knows the difference between 'context refresh' and 'web server start', and explains why ApplicationRunner runs after the port is open, is a stronger answer than any list of annotations.
bullets: Order: construct SpringApplication → load Environment → create context → refresh context (parse @Configuration, run BPPs, instantiate beans) → start embedded server → ApplicationRunner → ApplicationReadyEvent.
Environment is built from property sources in priority order: command-line > env vars > application-{profile} > application.yml > defaults.
Context refresh is where most failures happen: bean instantiation, auto-configuration, AOP wrapping, and the web server start all occur here.
ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner run AFTER the server is listening — exceptions here trigger shutdown of an already-started app.
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true trades startup speed for first-request latency and delayed failure detection.
--debug prints an auto-configuration report listing positive and negative condition matches — best tool for 'why was this bean not created?'
